title_en: Microsoft Now Claims Xbox Project Helix is a 'Console That Plays PC Games' Rather Than a Gaming PC
summary_en: Ever since Microsoft first teased its next-generation console/PC hybrid last year, there's been a lot of speculation on what Project Helix even is. And while that speculation is going to continue until Microsoft actually reveals the next-gen Xbox, the company has shed a bit more light on what we can expect.
body_en:
Ever since Microsoft first teased its next-generation console/PC hybrid last year, there's been a lot of speculation on what Project Helix even is. And while that speculation is going to continue until Microsoft actually reveals the next-gen Xbox, the company has shed a bit more light on what we can expect.
As part of its 25th anniversary celebration, Microsoft put out a special "Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine" that covered everything from the new Xbox Nano controller to World of Warcraft Forever . But the issue also had a huge story on "The Soul of Project Helix" where Xbox VP of Next Generation (that's a real job title) Jason Ronald gave a bit more detail on what Helix actually is.
Back when Sarah Bond revealed the partnership behind the "next generation hardware," she emphasized that Xbox was working with the Windows team to make the desktop OS "the number one platform for gaming." Ever since then, the assumption was that Helix would be something akin to a gaming PC . But in the Xbox 25th Anniversary Magazine, Ronald states clearly that "Helix is designed to be a console that is also capable of playing games from your PC. It is not a PC that can also play console games."
The goal, instead, is "making it easy, intuitive and instant to access my games." But while the focus is on creating a console, Ronald still says "if you're a hardcore gamer or a power user who wants to have that deeper level of customizability across settings and performance options, you can absolutely go do it."
It's impossible to tell exactly what Ronald is describing, here, though. Because Project Helix will be able to run PC games, there is a certain amount of freedom that it has to give users, otherwise Microsoft could unintentionally lock players out from parts of their game library, especially on some of the lesser-known PC game platforms. It doesn't sound like Microsoft wants to stop anyone from playing any of their games. Instead, Ronald said he wants to "remove the arbitrary constraints between console and PC games."
In reality, the Project Helix operating system is probably going to be some kind of branch off of Windows 11, and is going to take some of the DNA from the ROG Xbox Ally X. As Ronald puts it, "The ROG Xbox Ally was really an opportunity for us to learn alongside our player base with a lot of these concepts and the ideas that we had: being able to play libraries from across multiple different storefronts, understanding how PC games and console games can show up together in a unified library."
I have used the Xbox Ally X a ton over the last year, and while a lot of the bones of a console-like experience are there, I'm not sure it'll ever fully translate to the kind of polish you see on the Xbox Series X homepage. And Ronald is aware of that, too.
"The feedback that we've gotten from players has fundamentally informed and altered our plans of how it actually shows up in a future console," Ronald said. "Players shared where we met the mark and areas we needed to improve or approach differently. So absolutely, we view the Ally as a precursor to what we're doing with Helix – but it's informed by a lot of the design concepts we have for Helix."
The biggest concern for the next generation of consoles isn't really which operating system they're running on, or whether you can run Excel – the question is the pricing, and it's not looking pretty. While Ronald does try to talk around the prices, it still doesn't sound like Project Helix is going to be especially affordable.
"It's definitely a challenging time," he continued, "but as a system and platform designer it's also one of the most exciting times, because we have to invent entirely new technology to continue to advance the state-of-the-art while also continuing to make things accessible and affordable." I guess we'll see just how "accessible and affordable" the console is when it actually gets unveiled – however long that's going to take.
It also seems like Microsoft is using the RAM crisis to justify the need for neural rendering in Project Helix, as well. When talking about price, Ronald says, "This is a big reason why we're really focused on advancements like neural rendering, because it's an entirely new way to generate a frame without requiring more computational horsepower, additional memory, and things like that."
For the uninitiated, Nvidia's DLSS 5 is a major example of neural rendering tech that's actually made it to mainstream games like NBA 2K27 and Hogwarts Legacy. The idea is to improve visual quality in games by using AI to enhance images within the rendering pipeline. And it sure sounds like that tech is coming to the next-generation Xbox in one way or another.
My hope is that they keep it optional. No matter how you feel about DLSS 5, it does have a massive impact on performance while altering the way a game looks. Luckily, in the official implementations so far, it's been a relatively minor change, but there are definitely some modders who have pushed the technology to comical levels.
With the way that graphics tech is moving lately, there's no telling what Project Helix will be capable of until it's actually in our hands. I hope that Microsoft does go for an operating system that feels at home on a TV. I was worried that it would just lean on the Xbox full screen experience, and it just isn't there yet. At least it sounds like no matter how the OS feels to navigate with a controller, it's still focused on giving people finer controls over how the system runs. And if Microsoft plans to lean on tech like neural rendering and frame generation, that's going to be more important than ever.
Jackie Thomas is the Senior Tech Editor at IGN and the PC components queen. She's been covering gaming hardware for more than a decade for IGN, TechRadar, Gizmodo, PC Gamer and more. You can follow her  @Jackiecobra
